newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Fire illustrates Saudi fears of haj tragedies.
newsitem.headline: Fire illustrates Saudi fears of haj tragedies.

text.p: The latest tragedy to mar the sacred haj ritual, a wild fire that killed at least 217 pilgrims, reinforced the Saudi view that Moslem countries should stick to a quota system to avert disaster.
As custodian of Islam's two holiest shrines, the kingdom is faced with the daunting task of managing some two million Moslems, half of them arriving from abroad, during haj.
The blaze on Tuesday spread panic among thousands of pilgrims performing one of Islam's prime duties as it swept through 70,000 white tents in the Mena plain, 11 km (7 miles) from Mecca.
Riyadh said 217 died and over 1,290 were injured and diplomats struggled to get fresh casualty figures.
"There is always a sense of resignation. They always urge pilgrims to take precautions but accidents do happen," Indian ambassador to Riyadh Mohammad Hamad Ansari told Reuters.
Saudi authorities are still haunted by memories of several recent disasters, including a 1990 stampede in which 1,426 pilgrims were crushed to death in a tunnel.

They have been especially vigilant to prevent a repeat of the violence that rattled the haj in 1987, when 402 people, mostly Iranians, died in clashes with Saudi security forces at an Iranian-led rally.
Saudi Pilgrimage Minister Mahmoud bin Mohammad Safar said this month Moslem countries should continue to adhere to the quota "which aims to safeguard the interests and safety of pilgrims".

The number of pilgrims performing the haj each year is governed by quotas set in 1988 by the Organisation of the Islamic Conference based on a country's population. Saudi Arabia says the scheme, questioned by some states, eases congestion.
But the Saudis have learned that looking after throngs of men wrapped in simple white sheets and women in veils is much harder than merely imposing a quota system on paper.
People who have performed the haj say pilgrims, moving shoulder to shoulder, often carry everything from small gas stoves, to food to prayer mats.

Pilgrims often sit in vast rows of tents, like the ones engulfed in Tuesday's blaze, boiling pots of tea and coffee and cooking meat, vegetables and rice. It is a recipe for disaster in desert temperatures which this year soared to 40 Celsius (104 Fahrenheit).
The Saudi authorities also have to grapple with more than human error. Iran has for years objected to the quota system and said it was a Saudi pretext to limit the number of Iranians.
But the latest tragedy to hit the haj, one of the five pillars of Islam required of able-bodied pilgrims, did not delay the centuries-old ritual.
Workers cleared the debris left by raging flames as two million Moslems travelled on Wednesday to Mount Arafat where they pray to mark the climax of haj.
Pilgrims moved past charred refrigerators, air conditioners and clothes amid the lingering smell of smoke. A few security men looked over the blackened plain.
The spirits of the pilgrims seemed to rise. Some waved to cameras as they listened to a blind cleric deliver a sermon broadcast live on Saudi television.
He called for obedience to God and piety. An elderly man sat on the ground beside a coffee pot with the Moslem holy book, the Koran, in his lap.
